name: Beth Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and have answered calls and chats at this contact centre for years. I finished secondary school and can handle most billing disputes without help, though I'm not the best on the floor. The pay is low for this job. I keep a paper handover book because an unfinished case shouldn't disappear between shifts, and I have never used AI tools.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a shift need to cover at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Paul loads vans, and his hours vary. We have a mortgage, two school-age children aged eight and twelve, and less than a month's expenses saved. There are few similar jobs nearby. One missing shift changes what we can pay that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the day shift that a faster template is fine if we still have time to read a complaint. Someone must check the bill before the answer goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've done calls for years and usually know where to look, but the wage here is low. We have less than a month's expenses saved. A missed shift is a mortgage problem even without major AI change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my regular calls and write down disputed charges in the paper handover book. From this payday through the first year, Paul and I will stop the bought lunches at work and put what is left toward the house buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, though the work itself feels steady. I don't need a new screen to have a bill worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose wages pay the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paul loads delivery vans, and our children are eight and twelve. His hours change with the order book, so I cannot call my lower wage pocket money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use the suggestion box?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used the AI suggestion box. I read the account and ask the next experienced agent when a rule has changed.

say: I'd allow **faster templates** only with time to read the complaint.
I'd insist someone **checks the bill** before answering.
think: I feel **experienced** on calls but underpaid.
I fear one **missed shift** because we have less than a month saved for the mortgage.
do: Keep handling **regular calls** and writing paper handovers.
Put the freed money toward a **house buffer** through the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about money, with work still steady.
S0.quote: A missed shift is a mortgage problem even without major AI change.
fieldNote: Her **low pay** and very thin cushion predate any major AI shock.
She uses **paper handovers** and has never used AI tools.
Paul's **variable loading hours** make both earnings essential.

steps.text: Keep answering regular calls and recording disputed charges by hand
Put saved lunch money toward a mortgage buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the staff group to get the centre's paid-hour plan in writing before routine calls move. I want a person available when an automated answer makes a bill worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own hours could fall despite years on this desk. Other centres nearby are scarce, and Paul's loading wage is already uneven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll bring last month's rota to the staff meeting and ask two colleagues to compare theirs. If my hours shrink in the first year, I'll apply for a posted paid canteen assistant job at the school only if its wage and hours cover our mortgage; until then I'll stay on my current shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Years at the contact centre won't create a new paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your group ask management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask for paid hours, not just call counts, so management cannot say the queue looks healthy while pay falls. I would not ask one new agent to raise that alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the school offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the school what the whole week pays after travel. A friendly offer for two lunch hours would not cover our mortgage.

say: I'd ask our **staff group** for a written paid-hour plan.
I'd demand a **human appeal** when an automated bill answer is wrong.
think: I expect my **hours** could fall despite experience.
I know **few local centres** and Paul's uneven wages limit our fallback.
do: Compare **monthly rotas** with two colleagues at the staff meeting.
Keep my **current shift** while it pays.
Apply for a **posted paid school job** after cuts only if wages and hours cover mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost hours, low savings and scarce local jobs.
S1.quote: Years at the contact centre won't create a new paid shift.
fieldNote: Her **years of experience** do not protect a low-paid shift from cuts.
The **rota comparison** is collective, not a private complaint.
She rejects a **two-hour offer** that cannot cover the mortgage.

steps.text: Compare paid-hour rotas with two colleagues at staff meeting
Keep working current contact-centre shifts while they pay
Apply for posted paid school work after cuts only if wages and hours cover mortgage
Check full-week school pay after travel before accepting the offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the whole floor that general AI by 2028 could answer the calls we are paid for. Robots around 2031 do not buy a headset worker another three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my job could end, and our reserve is under one month. My partner Paul cannot carry the mortgage and two schoolchildren on uncertain van-loading hours by himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll join the staff group asking for written notice and a common answer about final pay. If my centre job ends in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for posted paid school-canteen work only if wages and hours cover the mortgage, and we'll cancel our planned holiday before using the house money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed enough to wake early. I have a plan to ask, not enough money to wait quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children we are staying home for the holiday and that both adults are still looking after the house. I would not make them carry the fear of a letter from work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could family cover a wage gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my sister about one week's groceries only if a wage gap leaves the food bill short. She has her own children, so I would check whether she can help before counting a penny.

say: I'd warn **2028 general AI** could remove paid call work.
I'd say **2031 robots** give headset workers no extra time.
think: I expect my **job could end** with less than a month saved.
I know Paul's **loading wage** cannot support our mortgage alone.
do: Join the **staff group** seeking written notice and final-pay terms.
Apply for **posted paid canteen work** after a cut only if wages and hours cover mortgage.
Cancel our **planned holiday** before spending the house reserve.
feel: **Alarmed** by a near-term job loss and almost no reserve.
S2.quote: My partner Paul cannot carry the mortgage and two schoolchildren on uncertain van-loading hours by himself.
fieldNote: Her **group request** seeks common notice and final-pay terms.
She avoids counting **sisterly help** until the need and availability are real.
She cuts a **holiday** before drawing on house money.

steps.text: Ask with staff group for written notice and final-pay terms
Apply for posted paid canteen work after cuts only if wages and hours cover mortgage
Cancel planned family holiday before drawing on house reserve
Ask sister for one grocery week only if wages leave food short and she can help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the staff group to press for five years of honest staffing dates and paid learning, not course posters. Our calls face full AGI in 2031; hands-on robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep earning while learning what a school kitchen actually requires. The children's school is nearby, but I won't call a canteen job safe forever when robots follow later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep my calls and ask the school about a posted paid assistant place with full enough hours. If it has a real opening, offers paid training and covers our mortgage, I'll complete its required food-safety course during paid time; in the first year after 2031 I'll move only on a written offer that still meets those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more room to check the numbers. Five years could let me learn without betting next month's mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check at the kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd visit the kitchen on a busy day and ask what the start time and lifting look like. I wouldn't pay for a certificate merely because it appeared in a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check with Paul?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Paul to compare school pickup and his van rota before we accept any new shift. A wage on paper is no use if one of us must leave work to collect our children.

say: I'd ask our **staff group** for dates and paid learning.
I'd separate **2031 call risk** from 2034 hands-on robots.
think: I could test **school kitchen work** while keeping wages.
I doubt the **later robot date** makes canteen work permanently safe.
do: Keep my **contact-centre calls** while they pay.
Complete **paid food-safety training** only for a posted school job with mortgage-covering wages and hours.
Move after 2031 only on a **written paid offer** whose hours and wages cover mortgage and school pickup.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to check the paid path.
S3.quote: A wage on paper is no use if one of us must leave work to collect our children.
fieldNote: Her **course gate** requires a posted opening, paid learning and sufficient wages.
The **school pickup** can erase an apparently good offer.
She keeps **current wages** until a written alternative exists.

steps.text: Keep taking paid centre calls while current shifts remain
Complete paid food-safety course only for posted school opening with mortgage-covering wages and hours
Move only on written paid school offer whose wages and hours cover mortgage and pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets the staff group bargain for fair notice and paid skills while wages still come in. Our phones face general AI in 2036; hands-on robots come around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might still owe on the mortgage and might still be helping the children. I would rather save while we can than assume either bill will vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep answering calls, put a fixed sum from each pay into the house account, and compare paid hours with colleagues once a quarter. If AGI arrives in 2036, I'll apply in its first year for a posted paid school job only if my hours end and the new wage and hours cover our mortgage and school travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Ten years lets me do small things, but our thin cushion is a worry right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new agent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a new agent to keep records of actual paid hours. The centre can praise service all day, but a mortgage needs a paycheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We won't move house for an imagined opening. Paul and I would need a written job offer and a school route we can manage before we even discuss it.

say: I'd ask for **fair notice** and paid skill-building over the decade.
I'd distinguish **2036 call work** from robots around 2039.
think: I might still owe a **mortgage at 53**.
I cannot assume the **children's costs** will vanish on schedule.
do: Keep my **current calls** while the shift pays.
Save a **fixed sum** from each pay for the house.
Apply for a **posted paid school job** only after call cuts and if wages and hours cover mortgage and travel.
S4.quote: The centre can praise service all day, but a mortgage needs a paycheque.
fieldNote: Her **current shortage** keeps the mood anxious despite a decade.
She compares **paid hours** with colleagues, not service slogans.
Any **family move** needs a written offer and workable school route.

steps.text: Keep answering paid calls while shifts remain
Save fixed sums from each pay into house account
Compare paid hours quarterly with contact-centre colleagues

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Call work could go while our mortgage and school bills stay, and we have less than a month saved. Written notice for every shift and a posted paid opening with enough hours would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who takes the call when a machine makes a payment mistake. Somebody should be paid to correct the account, and the customer needs a person to reach. I won't tell them a blank screen is an answer.

headlineQuote: Somebody should be paid to correct the account, and the customer needs a person to reach.
portrait: Beth is an **experienced 43-year-old agent** with secondary schooling and average job skill, handling billing disputes at a contact centre.
Her **low pay**, savings below one month and few local centres sit beside a mortgage and two school-age children.
Her partner's **variable loading hours** add household risk; she avoids AI tools and records handovers on paper.
She uses the **staff group** to seek notice and paid hours, and requires real school work before retraining or moving.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her calls while mortgage and school bills continue.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** for every shift would let the household plan.
A **posted paid school job** with enough hours and wages would permit a move.
